## Key relations

The **external quantum efficiency** counts collected electrons per incident photon, and the **responsivity** converts it to
amperes per watt (slides 21–22):

$$
\eta_e=\frac{I_{ph}/e}{P_o/h\nu},\qquad
\mathcal R=\frac{I_{ph}}{P_o}=\eta_e\frac{e}{h\nu}=\eta_e\frac{e\lambda}{hc}=\eta_e\,\frac{\lambda\,[\mu\text m]}{1.24}\ \text{A/W}.
$$

An ideal photodiode ($\eta_e=1$) has $\mathcal R$ growing linearly with λ up to the cut-off $\lambda_g$, then falling to zero
(slide 24). Real photodiodes lose photons by reflection at the surface (transmission $T$), by absorption in regions from which
carriers are not collected, and by transmission through the device. With the **internal quantum efficiency** $\eta_i$ (pairs per
absorbed photon, slide 28) and the useful (collecting) region between $x_1=\ell_p-L_e$ and $x_2=\ell_p+W+L_h$ (slides 139–144):

$$
I_{ph}=\frac{e\eta_iTP_o}{h\nu}\left[e^{-\alpha x_1}-e^{-\alpha x_2}\right],
\qquad \text{pin with thin p}^+:\ I_{ph}\approx\frac{e\eta_iTP_o}{h\nu}\left[1-e^{-\alpha W}\right].
$$

At short λ (large α) light is absorbed in the p⁺ layer and near the surface, where carriers recombine; at long λ (small α) it
passes through the collecting region. The responsivity peaks in between. Because $\eta_e=\mathcal Rhc/e\lambda$, the QE is
maximum where $d(\mathcal R/\lambda)/d\lambda=0$, i.e. where $d\mathcal R/d\lambda=\mathcal R/\lambda$: **the tangent to the
$\mathcal R(\lambda)$ curve passes through the origin** (slide 26). That point is not the peak of $\mathcal R$.

## Live panel: responsivity from the device structure (slides 27, 139–145)

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {alpha, MATERIALS, responsivity, fresnelT, structureR, qeff} from "./det_sim.js"
viewof rs = Inputs.form({
  mat: Inputs.select(Object.keys(MATERIALS), {value: "Si", label: "absorbing material"}),
  lp: Inputs.range([0.01, 3], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "p⁺ layer ℓ_p (µm)"}),
  Le: Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "electron diffusion length in p⁺, L_e (µm)"}),
  W: Inputs.range([0.5, 200], {value: 30, step: 0.5, label: "depletion width W (µm)"}),
  Lh: Inputs.range([0, 200], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "hole diffusion length in n, L_h (µm)"}),
  ar: Inputs.radio(["no coating (Fresnel)", "perfect AR coating"], {value: "no coating (Fresnel)", label: "surface"}),
  etai: Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "internal QE η_i"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rsOut = {
  const m = MATERIALS[rs.mat], T = rs.ar.startsWith("perfect") ? 1 : fresnelT(m.n), lg = 1.23984 / m.Eg, pts = [], ideal = [];
  let best = {eta: 0}, peak = {R: 0};
  for (let i = 0; i <= 600; i++) {
    const wl = (0.3 + (lg * 1.05 - 0.3) * i / 600) * 1e-6, a = alpha(rs.mat, wl);
    const R = structureR(wl, a, rs.lp * 1e-6, rs.W * 1e-6, rs.Le * 1e-6, rs.Lh * 1e-6, T, rs.etai);
    pts.push({wl: wl * 1e9, R, c: "this structure"}); ideal.push({wl: wl * 1e9, R: wl * 1e6 <= lg ? responsivity(1, wl) : 0, c: "ideal (η = 1)"});
    const eta = qeff(R, wl); if (eta > best.eta) best = {eta, wl: wl * 1e9, R}; if (R > peak.R) peak = {R, wl: wl * 1e9};
  }
  return {pts: pts.concat(ideal), best, peak, T, lg};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 320, x: {label: "wavelength (nm)"}, y: {label: "responsivity (A/W)", grid: true, domain: [0, 1.4]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["this structure", "ideal (η = 1)", "slide 24 (read off)"], range: ["#e34948", "#2a78d6", "#0b0b0b"]},
  marks: [Plot.line(rsOut.pts, {x: "wl", y: "R", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2}),
          Plot.line([{wl: 0, R: 0}, {wl: rsOut.best.wl * 1.6, R: rsOut.best.R * 1.6}], {x: "wl", y: "R", stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
          Plot.dot([rsOut.best], {x: "wl", y: "R", r: 6, fill: "#1baf7a"}),
          rs.mat === "Si" ? Plot.dot([{wl: 450, R: 0.24}, {wl: 700, R: 0.45}, {wl: 940, R: 0.56}], {x: "wl", y: "R", r: 4, fill: "#0b0b0b", symbol: "square"}) : null]
})
```

Things to try with Si: shrink $W$ to 1 µm and $L_h$ to 10 µm (a p⁺n diode): the infrared response collapses. Make $W=30$ µm
and $L_h=0.1$ µm (a pin): it recovers (slide 145). Thicken the p⁺ layer to 2 µm: the blue response disappears, the "A versus B"
difference of slide 34. Add the AR coating: everything rises by $1/T\approx1.47$. The black squares are read off the commercial
curve of slide 24; a real Si photodiode also loses carriers to surface recombination, which this model only mimics with $\ell_p$.

## Worked examples, recomputed

> **Slide 25.** The Si photodiode of slide 24 peaks at 940 nm with $\mathcal R\approx0.56$ A/W and has 0.24 A/W at 450 nm. QE at
> both wavelengths? Intensity giving 10 nA on 1 mm² at the peak? **Slide 26.** QE at the tangent point X (700 nm, 0.45 A/W)?
> **Slide 36.** A Si pin of 0.4 mm diameter gives 56.6 nA under 0.1 mW cm⁻² at 700 nm: responsivity and QE?
> **Slides 149–150.** A Ge photodiode (Thorlabs FDG03) has its QE maximum at 1500 nm with 0.95 A/W.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-qe
#| tbl-cap: "Worked examples of slides 25, 26, 36 and 150."
Po36 = np.pi*(0.02)**2*0.1e-3          # W (cm² × W/cm²)
R36 = 56.6e-9/Po36
rows = [("s25: QE at 940 nm, R = 0.56 A/W", f"{dl.quantum_efficiency(0.56, 940e-9):.3f}", "0.74"),
        ("s25: QE at 450 nm, R = 0.24 A/W", f"{dl.quantum_efficiency(0.24, 450e-9):.3f}", "0.66"),
        ("s25: intensity for 10 nA on 1 mm²", f"{10e-9/0.56*1e9:.1f} nW/mm²", "18 nW/mm²"),
        ("s26: maximum QE at X (700 nm, 0.45 A/W)", f"{dl.quantum_efficiency(0.45, 700e-9):.3f}", "0.80"),
        ("s36: incident power", f"{Po36*1e6:.3f} µW", "0.126 µW"),
        ("s36: responsivity", f"{R36:.3f} A/W", "0.45 A/W"),
        ("s36: QE", f"{dl.quantum_efficiency(R36, 700e-9):.3f}", "0.80"),
        ("s150: maximum QE of the Ge photodiode", f"{dl.quantum_efficiency(0.95, 1500e-9):.3f}", "0.79")]
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["quantity", "computed", "slide"])
```

Note the apparent paradox of slide 25: at 450 nm the responsivity is less than half its peak value (0.24 versus 0.56 A/W), yet
the QE is 66 %, close to the 74 % of the peak. Responsivity favours long wavelengths simply because each photon carries less
energy: a watt of near-infrared light contains twice as many photons as a watt of blue light.

> **Slides 141–145 (Table 5.7).** p⁺n and pin photodiodes with $\ell_p=0.5$ µm, $L_e=0.1$ µm, $\alpha=10^5$ m⁻¹ at 800 nm,
> $\eta_i=T=1$, $P_o=1$ µW. p⁺n: $W=1$ µm, $L_h=10$ µm. pin: $W=30$ µm, $L_h=0.1$ µm.

```{python}
#| label: fig-structures
#| fig-cap: "Responsivity of the two structures of Table 5.7 over the whole Si absorption band, with a perfect AR coating. The pin wins in the infrared, where the 30 µm drift region still absorbs; both lose the blue in the 0.5 µm p⁺ layer. Dashed: tangents through the origin marking the maximum QE."
wl = np.linspace(350e-9, 1150e-9, 800); a = dl.alpha("Si", wl)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
ax.plot(wl*1e9, dl.responsivity(1, wl)*(wl < 1.107e-6), color=dl.INK2, lw=1, label="ideal")
for (lab, W, Lh), c in zip((("p⁺n", 1e-6, 10e-6), ("pin", 30e-6, 0.1e-6)), dl.PALETTE):
    R = dl.photocurrent_structure(1, wl, a, 0.5e-6, W, 0.1e-6, Lh)
    lx, Rx, ex = dl.max_qe_point(wl, R)
    ax.plot(wl*1e9, R, color=c, label=f"{lab}: max QE {ex:.0%} at {lx*1e9:.0f} nm")
    ax.plot([0, 1.5*lx*1e9], [0, 1.5*Rx], ls="--", lw=1, color=c)
ax.set(xlabel="λ (nm)", ylabel="R (A/W)", xlim=(350, 1150), ylim=(0, 0.95)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()
```

## Commercial photodiodes (slides 33, 49)

```{python}
#| label: fig-commercial
#| fig-cap: "Quantum-efficiency lines (dashed, slide 33) and the ideal pin responsivity of Si (30 µm), Ge (10 µm) and In₀.₅₃Ga₀.₄₇As (3 µm) absorbers with a perfect AR coating and a thin, transparent cap layer. The shapes reproduce slide 33: Si covers 400–1100 nm, InGaAs 900–1700 nm, Ge extends to 1800 nm but with a weak tail beyond its direct gap."
wl = np.linspace(300e-9, 1900e-9, 1000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
for eta in (1, 0.75, 0.5):
    ax.plot(wl*1e9, dl.responsivity(eta, wl), ls=":", color=dl.INK2, lw=1)
    ax.text(1880, dl.responsivity(eta, 1.88e-6), f"{eta:.0%}", fontsize=8, color=dl.INK2, va="bottom", ha="right")
for (m, W), c in zip((("Si", 30e-6), ("Ge", 10e-6), ("In0.53Ga0.47As", 3e-6)), dl.PALETTE):
    lp = 0.05e-6 if m != "In0.53Ga0.47As" else 0.0       # InGaAs is lit through a transparent InP cap
    ax.plot(wl*1e9, dl.photocurrent_structure(1, wl, dl.alpha(m, wl), lp, W), color=c, label=f"{m}, {W*1e6:.0f} µm")
ax.set(xlabel="λ (nm)", ylabel="R (A/W)", ylim=(0, 1.3)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()
```

The InGaAs curve rises abruptly at about 920 nm in real devices (slide 33) because the light enters through an InP cap or
substrate, which absorbs below 920 nm. Removing the substrate ("visible-extended InGaAs") restores the short-wavelength response.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Going further
- **Surface recombination.** Replace the dead layer $\ell_p-L_e$ by a proper solution of the diffusion equation in the p⁺ layer with
  a surface recombination velocity $S$: solve $Dn''-n/\tau=-G(x)$ with $Dn'(0)=Sn(0)$ and $n=0$ at the depletion edge, derive the
  collection probability of a carrier generated at depth $x$, and show that a passivated surface ($S\to0$) recovers the blue
  response. This is what "UV-enhanced" Si photodiodes do.
- **Resonant-cavity photodiodes.** Put a thin absorber ($\alpha d\ll1$) between two Bragg mirrors (Ch. 1). At resonance the QE becomes
  $\eta=\frac{(1+R_2e^{-\alpha d})(1-R_1)(1-e^{-\alpha d})}{(1-\sqrt{R_1R_2}\,e^{-\alpha d})^2}$. A 0.2 µm InGaAs
  layer can then absorb > 90 %, decoupling QE from transit time (@sec-pin). What is the price?
- **Waveguide photodiodes** absorb light travelling *along* the junction: the absorption length is millimetres while the drift length
  is 1 µm. They reach 100 GHz with $\eta>0.8$ and are standard in silicon photonics (Ge-on-Si). Relate the absorption length to the
  confinement factor Γ of Ch. 2 and 4.
- **Quantum efficiency above 100 %.** In Si at λ < 300 nm one photon can create two pairs (impact ionisation by the hot carrier,
  $\eta_i>1$). Why does this not violate energy conservation?
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Prove the tangent criterion of slide 26 by differentiating $\eta_e(\lambda)=\mathcal R(\lambda)hc/e\lambda$.
2. With the panel, design a Si pin whose responsivity at 905 nm exceeds 0.6 A/W. What is its minimum depletion width with and without
   an AR coating?
3. A datasheet quotes "R = 1.0 A/W at 1550 nm" for an InGaAs photodiode. Is that physically possible? What QE does it imply?
4. Why does the responsivity of the InAs photodiode of slide 35 *increase* towards long wavelengths before its cut-off, while the
   QE is nearly constant?
